UNIT I · LESSON 1.412 min read

Criminalization of Conduct in Cyberspace

A harmful online act is not automatically a particular offence. Match conduct, mental state, statutory ingredients, and lawful procedure.

Print / PDF
01

Conduct, mental state, and prohibited result

Criminal liability generally requires an act or illegal omission together with the mental element specified by the offence. Dishonesty, fraudulence, knowledge, intention, and consent have technical meanings. A failed login caused by a forgotten password is not equivalent to intentional unauthorized access. A misleading advertisement is not automatically the offence of cheating without the required dishonest inducement and other ingredients.

The IT Act contains computer-specific provisions such as section 43 damage, section 66 dishonest or fraudulent commission of specified acts, section 66C identity theft, and section 66D cheating by personation using a computer resource. General criminal provisions may also apply to conspiracy, forgery, extortion, or cheating. Avoid stacking charges solely because the word “cyber” appears in the complaint.

02

Authorization and consent have boundaries

Authorization can be limited by purpose, account, system, duration, and method. Permission to use a laptop for printing does not necessarily authorize copying a confidential database. “Without permission” in section 43 must be applied to the facts; a publicly reachable login page is not necessarily an invitation to access private records.

Consent to one use of personal information does not authorize every later use. Similarly, a person’s ability to open a publicly accessible URL does not make every scraping or investigative use lawful. Examine contractual restrictions, privacy rights, applicable law, and the investigative authority. Ethical review is especially important when research involves vulnerable people.

03

From allegation to charge sheet

Investigators should create an ingredient table: statutory element, supporting fact, evidence source, alternative explanation, and missing corroboration. For cheating by personation, identify the false identity, the communication, the dishonest intention, and the induced act. The account name alone rarely proves who typed a message.

Procedural safeguards remain relevant after identifying the offence. Check cognizability, territorial jurisdiction, limitation where applicable, and the version of the criminal law. BNSS section 534 contains savings, while BNS section 358 addresses continued operation of repealed enactments for specified prior matters. Do not mechanically use an old section number in a new case.

The idea to take with you

A policy violation can support context without proving every crime. The prosecution still has to establish the statutory elements with reliable evidence.
